title: W′ balance in intervals, attacks and crits
goal: Track W′ balance through intermittent efforts with the Skiba model, and explain why its refill rate is personal and only roughly right.

steps.title: Spend above CP, refill below
steps.text:
Races and intervals don't hold one power. The CP model handles this with two rules [[c:wbal-rules]]:

- **Above CP**, W′ is spent at P − CP joules each second, in a straight line.
- **Below CP**, W′ refills: fast at first, then ever more slowly, like the exponential curves of the units module. How fast varies a lot between people.

What is left at any moment is your [W′ balance](g:w-prime-balance). Intervals end in exhaustion when it reaches zero.

So four things set how long a session lasts: the power and length of the work bouts, and the power and length of the recoveries. Longer recoveries extend it; raising any of the other three shortens it [[c:four-factors]].

claims.text: W′ is assumed to be spent linearly above CP and refilled along a curve below CP, at rates that vary a lot between people.

evidence.quote: However, while the utilization of W′ may be assumed to be linear, studies indicate that the reconstitution of W′ may be curvilinear with kinetics that are highly variable between individuals.

claims.text: Tolerance in intervals depends on work power and duration and recovery power and duration: longer recoveries extend it, raising any of the other three shortens it.

evidence.quote: it can be shown that performance during intermittent exercise is related to four factors: the intensity and duration of the work intervals and the intensity and duration of the recovery intervals.

if one of PW, DW, or PR is increased while the other variables are held constant, exercise tolerance is reduced; however, if DR is increased while the other variables are held constant, exercise tolerance is increased.

steps.title: Skiba's refill formula
steps.text:
Skiba and colleagues (2012) turned the refill rule into numbers. W′ comes back exponentially, with a [time constant](g:time-constant) τ that is shorter the further below CP you recover. DCP is CP minus recovery power [[c:skiba-tau]]:

**τ = 546 × e^(−0.01 × DCP) + 316** (s)

| recovery power | DCP | τ |
|---|---|---|
| 20 W below CP | 20 W | ≈ 763 s |
| 100 W below CP | 100 W | ≈ 517 s |
| 250 W below CP | 250 W | ≈ 361 s |

Even very easy spinning gives τ of about 6 min, and after one τ only 63% of the spent W′ is back. A later version updates the balance second by second; this is what head units and training apps show [[c:skiba-realtime]].

claims.text: In Skiba's model the W′ refill time constant gets shorter the further recovery power is below CP: τ = 546 × e^(−0.01 × DCP) + 316 s.

evidence.quote: The time constants of W' recharge were negatively correlated with the difference between sub-CP recovery power and CP.
W′ was reconstituted more rapidly when PR was smaller

claims.text: A differential form of the W′ balance model updates the balance continuously and is used in software and wrist-worn devices.

evidence.quote: The Skiba2 model allows reconstitution to be calculated continuously, ultimately allowing a cyclist to view an estimation of their current W′ balance in real time
it has been adapted for popular use both in desktop computer software and on wrist-worn devices.

steps.title: How much W′ is back after 2 min?
steps.problem: A rider has CP 280 W. An attack spent 8 kJ of her W′. She then recovers for 2 min at 180 W. How much of the 8 kJ is back?
steps: W′ back = 0.207 × 8 kJ ≈ 1.7 kJ. About a fifth: 6.3 kJ is still missing.
A straight-line guess (120 ÷ 517 of the 8 kJ ≈ 1.9 kJ) gives too much: the refill curve is steepest at the start and keeps flattening.

steps.title: Attacks, intervals and crits
steps.text:
- **Attacks.** Each surge above CP takes a bite of W′; a rider who answers every move empties it. In Skiba's study, a racer's modelled W′ balance hit almost zero just as he dropped out [[c:wbal-race]].
- **Intervals.** Choose work and rest so that W′ is nearly empty on the last rep, not the third.
- **[Criteriums](g:criterium).** Every corner means a sprint out of it, with only seconds before the next. Recovering just below CP refills little (τ ≈ 763 s at 20 W below). 'Recovering' above CP refills nothing; W′ just drains more slowly [[c:no-refill-above]]. Sitting in the draft (in another rider's slipstream), well below CP between corners, is what saves W′.

claims.text: Applied to a competitive cyclist's race file, the W′ balance model predicted exhaustion at the point he abandoned the race.

evidence.quote: The model accurately predicted exhaustion of the W' in a competitive cyclist during a road race.
with the competitor abandoning the race when predicted W′ bal was approximately 1.5 kJ

claims.text: When recovery power stays above CP there is no net refill of W′, only slower spending.

evidence.quote: The W′ reconstitution time constant increased to non-physiological values (~7056 s) when the PR remained above CP, indicating no net recharge of W′ but merely a slower rate of W′ utilization in the recovery intervals compared with the work intervals.

steps.title: How far to trust W′ balance
steps.text:
The model is useful but rough; it has had mixed results so far [[c:wbal-mixed]].

- **τ is personal.** In elite cyclists, W′ came back faster than the formula predicts (τ about 112 s shorter), so it would call them empty too soon [[c:elite-faster]].
- **Two speeds of refill.** Recovery has a fast phase (τ about 20 s) and a slow one (about 6–7 min). One exponential misses the fast part and underrates short recoveries [[c:two-phase]].
- **It slows with repeats.** After hard bouts, refill gets slower, so a model fitted to fresh legs can overrate recovery late in a race [[c:repeat-slower]].

Errors run both ways. Read the balance as a guide for comparing efforts, not as a fuel gauge to the last joule.

claims.text: The W′ balance model has had mixed results so far.

evidence.quote: Despite the model's intuitive appeal, it has achieved mixed results thus far, in part due to a lack of clarity in its basis and calculation.

claims.text: In elite cyclists W′ recovered faster than Skiba's model predicts, with a time constant about 112 s shorter.

evidence.quote: Comparing modified τW' values against the SKIBA 2 τW' values showed a negative bias of 112 (46) s (mean ± 95% confidence limits), suggesting that athletes recovered W' faster than predicted by SKIBA 2
The current SKIBA 2 model is not appropriate for use in elite cyclists, as it underpredicts the recovery rate of W'.

claims.text: W′ recovery follows two phases, a fast one (τ about 20 s) and a slow one (τ about 6–7 min); a single exponential underestimates short recoveries.

evidence.quote: W' reconstitution kinetics were best described by a bi-exponential model consisting of distinct fast and slow phases.
time constant (τ) FC = 21.5 s; τ SC = 388 s
We showed that W' recovery from exhaustion follows a two-phase exponential time course that is dependent on aerobic fitness.
underestimated W' recovery for all durations below 5 min

claims.text: After a second exhausting bout, W′ refill was slower, through a longer slow-phase time constant.

evidence.quote: Following the second recovery, W' reconstitution reduced by 9.1 ± 7.3%, at 180 s and 8.2 ± 9.8% at 240 s resulting in an increase in the modelled τ SC to 716 s with τ FC unchanged.

debate.question: Is one exponential with a group-average τ good enough to track W′ in training and racing?

sides.position: Yes, as a working tool: it tracked a real race and the rise in VO2, and improved versions can fix its known weak points.
No: refill has two phases, differs between people and slows with repeated efforts, so a single group τ can mislead in either direction.

points: W′ is spent at P − CP above CP and refills along a curve below it; what is left is the W′ balance.
Longer recoveries extend an interval session; harder or longer efforts, or harder recoveries, shorten it.
Skiba: τ = 546 × e^(−0.01 × DCP) + 316 s, about 6 min for very easy spinning and much longer just below CP.
"Recovering" above CP refills nothing: in crits and bunch rides, get well below CP between efforts.
Refill is personal, two-phase and slows with repeats: use W′ balance as a guide, not a precise gauge.

variants.stem: A rider with CP 280 W repeats 1-min efforts at 400 W with 1-min recoveries at 150 W until she can't. Which single change lets her do more repeats?

options.why: Right: a longer recovery is the one change that increases tolerance; W′ has more time to refill.

options.text: Raise the recovery power to 200 W
options.why: A harder recovery is closer to CP, so W′ refills more slowly.
Each longer effort spends more W′, so she empties it sooner.

options.text: Raise the effort power to 410 W
options.why: More power above CP spends W′ faster each second.

variants.stem: A rider has W′ 22 kJ and CP 300 W. She attacks at 420 W for 40 s. What is her W′ balance at the end of the attack?

options.why: Right: balance = W′ − (P − CP) × time.
This takes away the whole work of the attack. Only the part above CP comes out of W′.
That is what the attack spent, not what is left.
This takes away P − CP in kJ without multiplying by the time.

variants.stem: A rider has W′ 18 kJ and CP 250 W. He sprints at 550 W for 20 s. What is his W′ balance at the end?

variants.stem: A rider with CP 300 W recovers at 200 W. What W′ refill time constant does Skiba's formula give?

options.why: That is 546 + 316: it treats e^(−0.01 × DCP) as 1, as if recovery were at CP.
That is only the constant 316; the exponential part was left out.
That is only the exponential part; 316 s still has to be added.

variants.stem: A rider has spent 10 kJ of W′. With τ = 500 s, how much is back after 2 min of recovery?

options.why: Right: refilled = spent × (1 − e^(−t/τ)).
That is the part still missing (spent × e^(−t/τ)), not the part refilled.
This treats refill as a straight line (t ÷ τ × spent). The curve flattens, so the true value is lower.
63% is what is back after one full τ; far less time has passed.

options.why: Right: refilled = spent × (1 − e^(−t/τ)).
That is the part still missing (spent × e^(−t/τ)), not the part refilled.
This treats refill as a straight line (t ÷ τ × spent). The curve flattens, so the true value is lower.

variants.stem: Between corners in a crit, a rider with CP 300 W holds 310 W "to recover" after each sprint. What happens to her W′ balance between corners?

options.text: It keeps falling, only more slowly than in the sprints
options.why: Right: 310 W is still above CP, so W′ is spent at 10 J each second; there is no refill.

options.text: It refills slowly, since 310 W is far below sprint power
options.why: Refill needs power below CP, not just below the last sprint.

options.text: It refills fast, as in the steep start of the curve
options.why: The fast early refill happens only below CP.

options.text: It stays the same until the next sprint
options.why: At 310 W she is 10 W above CP, so W′ keeps draining.

variants.stem: A crit racer with CP 300 W wants to have W′ left for the final sprint. Which plan best saves it?

options.text: Sit deep in the draft so power drops well below CP between corners
options.why: Right: the further below CP she recovers, the shorter τ and the faster W′ comes back.

options.text: Ride a smooth 305 W all race; 5 W over CP costs nearly nothing
options.why: 5 J each second for an hour is 18 kJ, a whole W′, and there is never any refill.

options.text: Recover at 290 W: just below CP refills nearly as fast as soft-pedalling
options.why: At 10–20 W below CP, τ is about 760–810 s, far slower than the roughly 360 s of very easy spinning.

options.text: Never go above CP out of the corners
options.why: In a crit that means being dropped; the aim is to refill between efforts, not to avoid them.

variants.stem: A triathlete with CP 240 W and W′ 15 kJ plans 4 × 2 min at 300 W. Each rep spends 7.2 kJ. To finish the 4th rep with W′ just at zero, how much must her three recoveries put back in total?

options.why: Right: she needs 4 × 7.2 = 28.8 kJ but has 15 kJ, so recoveries must return 28.8 − 15 = 13.8 kJ.
That is the total the reps spend; it forgets the 15 kJ she starts with.
That is one rep's cost, not the shortfall over four reps.
This assumes each recovery must fully refill one rep; she only needs to cover the shortfall.

variants.solution: Per rep: (300 − 240) × 120 = 7,200 J. Four reps: 28.8 kJ. Start: 15 kJ. Needed from recoveries: 28.8 − 15 = 13.8 kJ, about 4.6 kJ per recovery.

variants.stem: An elite rider's head unit shows her W′ balance at 0 kJ, yet 2 min later she wins the sprint. Most likely explanation?

options.text: Her W′ refills faster than the default formula assumes
options.why: Right: elite cyclists recovered W′ faster than Skiba's model predicts, so it called her empty too soon.

options.text: She sprinted on CP alone, with no W′
options.why: A sprint is far above CP, so it must spend W′.

options.text: Her CP must be lower than the unit thinks
options.why: A lower CP would make her look even emptier, not fresher.

options.text: Sprints use only PCr, which W′ doesn't include
options.why: PCr is part of what W′ represents; any power above CP spends W′.

variants.stem: Late in a hard race, after several exhausting efforts, how does W′ refill compare with the start of the race?

options.why: Right: after repeated exhausting bouts the slow phase of refill took longer.

options.text: It is faster, because the rider is warmed up
options.why: Warming up helps early efforts, but refill after repeated exhausting bouts slowed.

options.text: It is the same, since τ depends only on recovery power
options.why: In Skiba's formula it does, but measured refill slowed with repeats.
Refill slowed by about 8–9% at 3–4 min, not to zero.

variants.stem: Skiba's τ formula came from 7 recreationally active men doing 60-s efforts with 30-s recoveries on a lab ergometer. What most limits using it for an elite crit racer?

options.text: Seven non-elite men and one interval pattern: elite crit racing differs
options.why: Right: τ varies between people and protocols, and elite riders were shown to refill faster.

options.text: Lab ergometers measure power wrongly, so the numbers are invalid
options.why: Lab ergometers measure power well; the issue is who was tested and how.

options.text: It had no placebo group, so the formula can't be trusted
options.why: This was a modelling study; a placebo group would not answer its question.

options.text: It was published in 2012, so it must be out of date
options.why: Age alone doesn't make a study wrong; what limits it is the sample and the protocol.
